title: Salesforce Is Spending $300 Million on AI Tokens Instead of Hiring Engineers. For India's Tech Workforce, the Implications Are Vast.
excerpt: Marc Benioff's bet on Anthropic signals a structural shift in how software gets built — and who builds it. India's millions of IT workers should be paying close attention.
body:
When Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff appeared on the All-In podcast last week, he did not mince words. His company, he said, would spend approximately $300 million on Anthropic's AI tokens in 2026 — almost entirely for coding. He would not be hiring new software engineers. And he was thrilled about it.

"These coding agents are awesome. Anthropic is awesome," Benioff said. "Coding, everything's going to be cheaper to make. It's more efficient. I can do things that I just could not do before."

The statement, delivered with the enthusiasm of a convert, marks a watershed in how one of Silicon Valley's most influential companies thinks about its workforce. And for the millions of Indian engineers whose livelihoods depend on writing software for Western corporations, the implications are impossible to ignore.

## The Numbers Tell a Stark Story

Salesforce's internal data shows AI tools have boosted productivity by over 30 per cent across its engineering teams. By mid-2025, artificial intelligence was handling between 30 and 50 per cent of work across the company. The customer support division, once 9,000 people strong, has been trimmed to roughly 5,000 — the rest replaced by AI agents.

The $300 million earmarked for Anthropic is not a research experiment. It is an operating expense, a line item that directly substitutes for the salaries of engineers who will never be hired. Benioff framed it as a new operating model: "Today, I have humans, agents, and headless platforms all interoperating. Never before."

Meanwhile, Anthropic itself has become a juggernaut. Its annualised revenue surged from $1 billion in early 2025 to over $30 billion by April 2026 — a pace Salesforce took nearly two decades to match. Anthropic did it in under three years.

## What This Means for India's IT Empire

India's information technology services sector — a $254 billion industry employing more than 5.4 million people — is built on a foundational assumption: that writing and maintaining software requires large teams of skilled human engineers. Companies like TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and HCLTech have turned that assumption into a global business model, placing Indian developers in offshore centres that serve Fortune 500 clients.

Salesforce's pivot does not merely threaten that model. It rewrites the economics entirely. If a single company can redirect $300 million from human payroll to AI tokens and see productivity gains, every CTO and CFO at every major client will be asking the same question: why are we paying for headcount when we could be buying compute?

The early signals are already visible. Salesforce itself announced it would hire up to 2,000 new salespeople even as it froze engineering recruitment — a shift from building products to selling AI-powered ones. For Indian IT firms, whose margins depend on deploying large engineering teams, this is an existential challenge.

## Not Extinction, but Transformation

Industry leaders in India have been quick to position this as evolution rather than elimination. Nasscom has argued that AI will create new categories of work — AI trainers, prompt engineers, model evaluators — even as it displaces traditional coding roles. Some of India's largest IT firms have already begun retraining programmes, pivoting engineers toward AI-adjacent skills.

But the pace of change is outstripping the pace of adaptation. Benioff himself acknowledged that engineers at Salesforce are not being fired — they are being repositioned as supervisors of AI-generated code. "The engineers are still here," he said. "They're just doing different work."

The question for India is whether its workforce can make that transition fast enough. The country produces roughly 1.5 million engineering graduates each year, many of them trained in exactly the kind of manual coding work that AI agents are beginning to automate. The pipeline was built for a world that is disappearing.

## The Broader Pattern

Salesforce is not alone. The company's decision sits within a broader industry trend: LinkedIn announced layoffs across multiple departments globally, Standard Chartered plans to cut 7,800 jobs by 2030 with India's back-office workforce in the crosshairs, and Meta has shifted 7,000 employees into AI roles while cutting 8,000 others.

For NRIs working in American tech companies on H-1B visas, the anxiety is immediate and personal. Hiring freezes and restructurings disproportionately affect roles that were traditionally filled by Indian workers — quality assurance, backend development, systems integration. The very jobs that powered a generation of Indian-American upward mobility are being re-evaluated.

## What Comes Next

Benioff's $300 million bet is a signal, not a verdict. AI-generated code still requires human oversight, and the complexity of enterprise software means experienced engineers will remain essential for years. But the direction is unmistakable: the economics of software development are shifting from labour to capital, from headcount to compute.

For India's technology sector — and for the diaspora professionals who built their careers within it — the task is no longer to debate whether this shift is real. It is to figure out how to be on the right side of it.
